name: Module 1 - Introduction to Amazon FBA (Wholesale & Bundling)

blocks.content: Module 1: The Blueprint to 6-Figures
If you have never sold anything online before, the world of Amazon can look like a maze of confusing jargon. Let us strip all of that away.

To build a successful business on Amazon, you do not need to own a massive warehouse, you do not need a fleet of delivery trucks, and you do not need to spend your days packing and sending off customer orders.

Amazon has already spent billions of pounds building the most advanced delivery network on the planet. FBA stands for Fulfilment by Amazon. When you use FBA, you are simply renting a tiny corner of their infrastructure.
The Core Concept: Split the Work
An Amazon FBA business is a partnership between you and Amazon. You handle the digital side; Amazon handles the physical side.

The Lean Reality: because Amazon handles the physical shipping, once you have shipped your products to Amazon you can run this entire business from anywhere in the world with nothing more than a smartphone and a laptop.
The Ultimate Superpower: The Prime Badge

There are two ways to sell on Amazon. The first is FBM (Fulfilment by Merchant), where you handle the whole physical chain yourself. You buy the stock, you store it at home or in a small unit, you print the postage labels, you queue at the post office, and you personally answer every customer message when something goes wrong with an order.

It is slow, it is exhausting, and customers do not trust it the way they trust an Amazon shipment. FBM listings show a generic delivery window of three to seven working days. They have no Prime badge, no guaranteed next-day delivery, and no Amazon-backed returns policy. A buyer comparing two identical products at the same price will pick the Prime listing every single time, even when the FBM version is a few pounds cheaper.

This is exactly why the Elite FBA System uses FBA and not FBM. We do not want to be the warehouse, the post office, and the customer service desk all at once. We want to be the buyer and the strategist. FBA hands the entire physical operation over to Amazon's billion-pound logistics network and gives us our time back to focus on what actually moves the business forward: finding the next profitable product.

Mechanically, FBA is very simple. You ship a single box of stock to an Amazon fulfilment centre. Their staff unload it, scan each unit, and check it into your inventory. From that point on, every customer order is picked off the shelf, packed into an Amazon box, shipped under the Amazon brand, and tracked by Amazon's own systems. If a buyer wants to return it, they speak to Amazon, not to you.

The moment your stock arrives at an Amazon FBA warehouse and is scanned in, your products automatically get the Amazon Prime badge. There is no application form, no waiting list, and no extra fee on top of the standard FBA fees you are already paying. Within a few hours, your listings are live and visible to every Prime customer searching for that product.
Tap each unlock below to see why that single badge is the difference between a listing that sells and a listing that does not.
How You Actually Make Money
The math behind Amazon FBA is straightforward. You are looking for simple price mismatches in the real world.

You do not need to guess if a product will make a profit. Before you spend a single penny on inventory, you will use free tools to calculate the exact Amazon fees and your exact profit margin. If the math does not work, you walk away.
Our Framework: The Lean Model
Most gurus will tell you to order 500 units of a custom product from China, spend £3,000 upfront, and pray it sells. We do not do that here. That is how beginners lose their life savings.
The Elite FBA method is built on a strict Lean, Validate, Scale framework. Click each step below to see how it works in practice.
Amazon FBA is simply a logistics machine. Once you understand how to slide products into that machine safely, the sky is the limit.
The Step-by-Step Infrastructure Flow
Getting products into the Amazon ecosystem requires a specific, orderly sequence. Following these steps correctly ensures that inventory is tracked accurately and processed without warehouse delays.
The Stow Algorithm and Inventory Health

Once your stock lands at the warehouse, Amazon's Stow algorithm splits your items across different physical shelves in the warehouse, and across different regional fulfilment hubs around the country. This ensures that no matter where a customer orders from, your product is always physically close to a picker, maximising delivery speed.
When looking at your Seller Central dashboard, monitoring stock levels across the three statuses below is a daily operational requirement to prevent stockouts or excessive storage fees.

⚠️ The 180-Day Penalty: if your stock sits in a warehouse for more than 180 days, Amazon charges severe Long-Term Storage Fees. This is why we use the Lean Model: we test with 10 to 12 units first. We never risk buying hundreds of units upfront without historical verification.
Behind the Scenes: The 24-Hour Fulfilment Machine

The moment a customer purchases your product, Amazon does not immediately release the funds to your bank account. They hold them in a temporary reserve to ensure there are no immediate returns or chargebacks. Payouts are typically initiated every 14 days.

While you sleep, work your day job, or spend time with family, this flawless automated machine runs 24 hours a day, 365 days a year. Tap any stage of the journey below to see what is happening behind the scenes.
Hands-Off Customer Service: Amazon's Automated Front Desk

When you use Amazon FBA, your job as a customer service representative is effectively eliminated. For a lean, individual operator, managing customer messages, tracking updates, and refunds can drain hours from your week. Amazon absorbs this entire infrastructure, acting as your customer service front desk 24 hours a day, 7 days a week.
Here is exactly how this hands-off layer operates in the real world.
Direct Customer Inquiries

If a buyer clicks Contact Seller to ask standard tracking questions like "Where is my parcel?" or "When will this arrive?", Amazon's support team intercepts the message. They handle the communication directly using their live carrier tracking data. You never see the message, and you do not have to reply to it.
The Refund and Return Automation

If a customer decides they no longer want your bundle, or if a product arrives damaged, they initiate a return through their own Amazon buyer dashboard. Amazon instantly issues a return shipping label, handles the refund processing out of your account's gross funds, and instructs the buyer to ship the physical item back to the fulfilment centre.
Inventory Disposition

Once the returned item arrives back at the warehouse, Amazon's staff inspect it. If the item is still pristine and unopened, they automatically put it back onto the shelf as Fulfillable Inventory to be sold again. If the packaging is torn or opened, they mark it as Unfulfillable, allowing you to recall it to your home address to inspect or salvage the components.

⚠️ The Operator Risk (the Return Rate Metric): while this system is completely hands-off, it is not free from risk. Amazon makes returning items incredibly easy for buyers. As an operator, you must track your Return Rate (total returns divided by total units sold) inside your seller dashboard. If you build poor-quality bundles that get damaged in transit, or if your listing images do not match the physical product exactly, your return rate will spike and put your account health at risk.
What the Prime Badge Really Is

Amazon Prime is the most successful paid subscription service ever launched. For a flat annual fee, members get fast and free shipping on hundreds of millions of products, plus video streaming, music, photo storage, exclusive sales events, and a long list of secondary perks. In the UK and the US, more than half of all households now hold a Prime membership.

On a product page, the badge itself looks deceptively small: a blue chevron mark next to the word Prime, usually sitting just above the price. But that tiny symbol is the single most powerful conversion signal Amazon has ever built. It tells the buyer that this item ships fast, it ships free, and if anything goes wrong, Amazon stands behind it personally.

For a third-party seller, the badge is the front door to the customer. Without it, your listing sits behind an invisible wall that millions of Prime buyers never look past. With it, your listing is funnelled into the same trusted pipeline as every other product Amazon recommends.
Why the Badge Wins Sales

The badge does the heavy lifting on three different levers at once: trust, search visibility, and pricing freedom. Each one alone would be valuable. Stacked together they are why an FBA listing routinely out-sells a cheaper FBM listing on the same product page.
The Trust Multiplier

Customers do not know who you are, and frankly, they don't care. When they see the Prime badge, their trust transfers directly from Amazon to your listing. They know that if the product is late, damaged, or not what they expected, Amazon's customer service will instantly handle it.
The "Next-Day" Filter

Over 80% of Amazon buyers filter search results strictly by "Prime Only." If you handle your own shipping (FBM / Fulfillment by Merchant), your listing becomes completely invisible to Amazon's most active, highest-spending customers.
Bypassing the Price Fight

Non-Prime sellers often have to lower their prices to get noticed. Because Prime members prioritize speed and reliability, they are consistently willing to pay a premium price. You can list a bundle for £19.99 and comfortably out-sell a non-Prime competitor offering a similar single item for less, simply because your product can be on their doorstep tomorrow morning.
How Prime Members Actually Behave

Prime membership is not a casual purchase. People who subscribe pay roughly £95 a year up front, and they actively want to use the perks to feel that the subscription has paid for itself. That single psychological shift changes everything about how they shop on Amazon.

They search differently. They filter for Prime first, often without even noticing the toggle is on. They have made Amazon their default starting point for many categories where, a decade ago, they would have used Google or visited a physical shop. And they trust Amazon's recommendations enough to one-click items they have never seen or heard of before.

📈 The Loyalty Loop: a Prime member who uses the badge to find a useful item is more likely to come back next week, more likely to add a second item to their basket, and more likely to leave a positive review. The badge does not just win a single sale; it triggers a repeating loop that compounds over months and years.
How a Listing Becomes Prime-Eligible
There are two official ways for a third-party seller to earn the Prime badge on a listing. In practice, only one of them is realistic for almost every seller, and that is FBA.

The second route, Seller-Fulfilled Prime, technically lets you keep stock at home and still display the Prime badge. In reality, it requires near-perfect on-time delivery from your own warehouse, a strict packaging audit, and continuous performance monitoring that almost no individual seller can sustain. Amazon has also paused new applications to the programme for years at a time to keep quality high.

🎯 The Practical Reality: for the Elite FBA System, the answer is simple. We always use FBA. The Prime badge appears automatically the moment our stock is scanned in, and we never have to worry about losing it because of a slow delivery, a missed dispatch, or a packaging audit.
The Cost of Using Amazon's Machine

Amazon does not store, pack, and ship your inventory out of goodwill. FBA is an elite infrastructure, but it is an infrastructure that will quietly bleed your bank account dry if you do not understand exactly how it charges you.

To protect your cash flow, you must understand the core fee layers deducted from every sale. As an operator, your job is to calculate these costs down to the penny before you spend a single pound on physical inventory. If you guess, you lose.
The Three Core Fees
Every time a customer clicks Buy Now on your listing, Amazon's system instantly calculates and deducts three distinct fee types before the remaining capital hits your account reserve.
1. The Referral Fee (The Marketplace Commission)
Think of this as your finder's fee. Amazon owns the customer data, the traffic, and the checkout platform; you are paying a direct commission for access to their active buyer base.

The Calculation: for almost every everyday category we target in the Elite FBA framework (Grocery, Beauty, Home, Personal Care, and Toys), this is a flat 15% of the total gross amount the customer pays at checkout.

💷 The Catch: this fee is calculated on the total retail price paid. If you sell a custom multipack for £19.99, Amazon instantly takes £3.00 the exact second the transaction processes. You never handle this money; it is sliced off at the point of sale.
2. The FBA Fulfilment Fee (The Logistics Cost)

This is the flat charge for Amazon's robotics and warehouse staff to physically pull your item off its warehouse shelf, track it, pack it into an official Amazon-branded cardboard box, and deliver it to the customer's doorstep.
The Calculation: this is based strictly on the weight and the physical outer dimensions of your finished, pre-packaged bundle. It has absolutely nothing to do with the retail price you charge.

📐 The Operator Rule: when sourcing inventory in physical retail shops, always look at items through the lens of volumetric weight. A bundle that can be packed tightly into a flat polybag or a slim mailer box will always make more money than an awkwardly shaped, hollow, or bulky item.
3. Monthly Storage Fees (The Rent)
You are renting high-value physical space inside Amazon's fulfilment centres. This space is measured and billed monthly per cubic foot (roughly 30cm × 30cm × 30cm).

Standard Storage (January to September): a low, highly predictable baseline operating cost. As long as your inventory turns over within our recommended 30 to 45 day window, this fee is negligible and barely impacts your net margins.

Peak Q4 Storage (October to December): during the holiday rush, millions of sellers flood the warehouses with inventory. To prevent gridlock and force slow-moving items out, Amazon triples their monthly storage fees.

🎯 The Operator Rule: if you have dead or unvalidated stock sitting on a warehouse shelf in November, storage fees will swallow your profits. This is exactly why the Elite FBA framework uses a lean setup: we test initial demand with only 10 to 12 units. We never buy hundreds of units upfront to sit around gathering dust and racking up penalty fees.
The Size Tier Trap

Amazon breaks products down into incredibly strict dimensional size categories. Moving just 1mm past a size tier boundary can instantly bump your fulfilment fee up by £0.50 to £1.50 per unit. That single millimetre can completely wipe out your projected net profit.

When you are bundling items together physically at your desk (for example, taping a 3-pack of specialised lightbulbs together), you are the manufacturer. How you position, wrap, and bag those items determines their final dimensions.

⚠️ Operator Warning: if you bag items loosely and leave excess plastic flagging out from the sides, Amazon's automated laser scanners (Cubiscan machines) will measure that empty plastic flagging as part of the solid product volume. You will be up-charged into a higher parcel tier for shipping trapped air. Wrap your bundles tight, tap down excess corners, and pack them as densely as humanly possible.
Real-World Bundle Scenarios
To help you visualise how these fee layers operate in action across different item types, analyse these three distinct operational scenarios based on common retail bundle configurations.
Understanding the Unit Economics

Unit economics is the per-sale profit and loss of a single product. It is the smallest meaningful financial unit in your business. Everything else, from the size of your Q4 storage bill to the speed of your cash compounding, is a downstream consequence of these numbers.

Operators do not look at revenue. Revenue is a vanity figure that hides the cost of running the business. They look at one number: how many pounds are left in their pocket after every single unit is sold, fees deducted, returns absorbed, and storage accounted for. If that number is healthy and repeatable, the business scales smoothly. If it is not, no amount of sales volume will save it.

💡 The Operator Mindset: a £100,000-a-year bundle that nets £0.50 per unit is a tax-only business. A £30,000-a-year bundle that nets £8 per unit is an actual operation. We optimise for the second every single time.
Single Item vs Bundle: The Real Math

The cleanest way to see why this framework works is to compare the per-unit economics of fighting for an existing single-product listing against running your own unique bundle. The figures below are pulled from a representative pair of listings: a generic car sponge sold on a crowded ASIN versus a bundle we built around it.

🎯 The Key Reframe: total Amazon fees on the bundle (£6.00) are only £2.50 higher than the single item (£3.50), yet net profit per unit is more than five times larger. Raising the Average Order Value through bundling makes Amazon's flat logistics fees work for you rather than against you.
The Three Levers of Healthy Bundle Economics

Every bundle in the Elite FBA framework is evaluated against three independent levers. Move any one of them in the right direction and your unit economics improve. Get all three pointing the right way and the bundle compounds into a genuine cash-flow asset rather than a side-project listing.
What Good Looks Like

Before sourcing any bundle, you run it through the floor rule. If the projected per-unit numbers do not clear all four thresholds at the same time on conservative assumptions, the bundle does not get built. This is the line between a hobbyist hunting for any sale and an operator running a real P and L.

⚠️ The Floor Is Not a Goal: hitting £5 net or 30% margin is the minimum threshold to even consider sourcing. A bundle that clears it by a hair will not survive a fee revision, a Q4 storage cycle, or a 5% return rate. Aim well above the floor, then sourcing decisions become easy.
The Compounding Effect

A single bundle running at the floor (around 60 units a month at £5 net) produces roughly £300 of net cash per month. Modest. The compound game is what happens when you have five, ten, or twenty of these running in parallel, each one validated, locked behind a brand registry, and replenished automatically from wholesale.

That is what good unit economics buy you. Not a single windfall but a quietly growing system that gets larger every month with no extra headcount, no extra customer service workload, and no extra retail real estate. Each bundle is an independent cash-flow engine running on the same warehouse infrastructure.
Where Unit Economics Go Wrong
Bundles that look great on a spreadsheet can collapse the moment they hit a real fulfilment centre. The most common failure modes show up in roughly the same shapes every time.

📐 The Tier-Tripping Bundle: the components nest beautifully on paper, but the polybag adds 3mm of slack and pushes the finished pack into the Standard Parcel tier. An extra £1.50 per unit on every sale, forever. Mitigation: measure the prototype with calipers and confirm the tier before sending anything in.

🐢 The Slow-Mover: net £8 per unit looks great until you realise the bundle sells two units a month. Storage fees, return processing, and stockout penalties eat the margin alive. Mitigation: validate velocity in Phase 2 of the blueprint before committing any wholesale capital.

❄️ The Q4 Crusher: a 25% margin in March becomes a 5% margin in November when Amazon triples storage fees. Mitigation: keep margins comfortably above 30% during validation, so peak season pressure still leaves something on the bone.

Unit economics is not a one-off calculation. It is the lens through which every sourcing decision, every wholesale negotiation, and every Q4 inventory buy is filtered. Master it on the validation bundle and the model carries forward to every bundle you build after it.

name: Module 2 - Opening your first Seller Account

blocks.content: Module 2: Opening Your First Seller Account

blocks.label: Before You Begin
blocks.description: The documents, accounts, and information you need ready before opening the signup wizard.

blocks.content: Why Preparation Beats Speed

Opening an Amazon Seller account looks like a 20-minute web form. It is not. It is a verification process that can take days or weeks depending on how prepared you are when you start. The fastest path through is not to rush; it is to walk in with every document, account, and answer already to hand.

Amazon's verification system runs strict identity, banking, and address checks. Any mismatch (a missing middle name, a slightly different address spelling, a card that triggers a 3D Secure prompt) sends you back to the start of a queue. New sellers who turn up unprepared spend 3 to 6 weeks bouncing between failed checks. Sellers who walk in prepared get verified in 5 to 10 business days.
🎯 The Operator Mindset: do not start the wizard before you have completed the checklist below. Every item missing at registration costs you a verification cycle. Every cycle is a week.
Your Pre-Flight Checklist

Work through the seven items below. Each one is required, each one needs to match the others, and each one will be checked by a human at some stage of verification. Tap a row to see the format Amazon expects.
Common Preparation Mistakes

Three small decisions before signup prevent the most common rejections later. Use a fresh email address that you have never used to shop on Amazon, otherwise the wizard sometimes confuses your shopper history with your seller registration. Make sure your name on the bank account exactly matches your passport, including middle names, before you start. And confirm the address on file with your bank is the same one you plan to register at, because the verification postcard will be cross-checked.
💡 Plan a 30-minute prep block: ID photos taken, bank statement downloaded as PDF, new business email created, dedicated mobile number ready. Then start the wizard in one uninterrupted sitting.

blocks.label: Choosing Your Selling Plan
blocks.description: Individual vs Professional. The cost trade-off, the hidden Buy Box rule, and when to switch.

blocks.content: Two Plans, One Decision

Amazon offers exactly two seller plans, and they look almost identical on the surface. The difference is a single line of fine print: only Professional sellers are eligible to win the Buy Box. That single line decides whether your bundle earns sales or sits invisible behind a 'Other Sellers' link.

On the Individual plan, you pay nothing per month but lose £0.75 per unit sold. On the Professional plan, you pay £25 plus VAT per month flat and keep every penny per unit. The break-even point is 33 units a month, which is roughly one a day.
Side-by-Side, Feature by Feature

The table below lets you switch between plans to see the eight features that actually matter. Tap the header of either plan to highlight its column. Note that four of the features are Professional-only, and three of those (Buy Box, ungating applications, Sponsored Ads) are essential for the Elite FBA framework to work at all.
The Two-Stage Sequence We Use

Our standard sequence is to open the account on the Individual plan, then upgrade to Professional the moment our first units are checked into the fulfilment centre. This costs nothing during the verification wait (often 5 to 10 days), and unlocks every Professional feature within minutes of upgrading. The upgrade itself is a single button in Account Settings > Manage Selling Plan.

There is no penalty for switching either direction, and Amazon does not require any re-verification when you do. The only thing to watch is the timing: if you upgrade on the first day of a calendar month, you pay the full £25 for that month. Upgrade on the 28th and you still pay the full £25. Pick your upgrade date strategically.

🎯 The Operator Move: do not upgrade until your test units are scanned into a fulfilment centre and your first listing is live. Until that point, you are paying £25 a month for features you cannot use.

blocks.label: Walking Through the Wizard
blocks.description: The eight-step signup process, broken down screen by screen with the exact fields to fill.

blocks.content: Before You Click Sign Up

Two final checks before opening the wizard. First, confirm you are on sell.amazon.co.uk in your browser address bar, not sell.amazon.com. The marketplace you start in becomes your home marketplace, and migrating later is painful. Second, sign out of any existing Amazon shopper account in the same browser, then open the seller signup in a fresh incognito window. This stops Amazon's session manager from confusing your shopper identity with your seller registration.

Plan for 30 minutes of uninterrupted form-filling once you start. The wizard saves progress automatically, but having to leave halfway through and come back invites verification edge cases (timing out, regenerating session tokens) that are hard to recover from.
The Eight Steps, in Order

Tap each numbered step below to see exactly what Amazon asks for, the fields you fill in, and the most common watch-out on that step. Steps 1 to 6 are form-filling. Step 7 is the video call. Step 8 is the postcard wait.
After You Submit

Once you click the final Submit, Seller Central opens immediately in a partly-active state. You can browse the menus and start drafting listings, but you cannot list anything live, accept payments, or send inventory to Amazon until verification completes. This wait is normal. Use it productively by drafting your first listing in the Catalog menu (covered in Module 4) so it is ready to publish the moment verification passes.

You will receive emails at three milestones: when the documents pass automated review, when the video call is scheduled, and when the address postcard is sent. If any of these emails do not arrive within their expected window (24 hours, 3 business days, 7 business days respectively), check the Performance > Account Health page in Seller Central for any required action.

blocks.label: Verification & Approval
blocks.description: What Amazon checks, the video call, common rejection patterns, and how to recover from a suspension.

blocks.content: What Amazon Is Actually Checking

Amazon's verification is not a credit check or a business audit. It is an identity check designed to prevent three specific abuses: fraudsters opening accounts with stolen IDs, previously-banned sellers returning under new identities, and bots farming accounts at scale. Knowing which threat the check is designed to catch helps you understand why every single field matters.

The verification has three layers. The automated layer checks document images for editing artefacts and runs OCR to extract name, address, and date of birth. The human layer is a verification associate who looks at your documents and matches them against the form data. The video layer is a 30-minute call where a verifier confirms you, the person on camera, are the same person on the ID and the same person typing the answers.
The Video Call, Step by Step

Amazon schedules the video call after the document upload passes automated review. Slots are usually 30 minutes long and offered within 2 to 5 business days of submission. The call takes place on Amazon Chime, in your browser. You do not need to install anything. You will be asked to hold your physical ID up to the camera at eye level, answer a few sourcing questions (what you plan to sell, where you plan to source from), and confirm a handful of details from the form.

The verifier is checking for three things. One: do you look like the person on the ID? Two: are you answering naturally or reading from a script? Three: does the room and setup look like a real workspace, not a coaching session? Sit in good even light, have your physical ID and any backup documents on the desk, and answer in your own words. Verifiers are trained to catch rehearsed answers.
💡 If you stumble on a question (forgetting your own UTR is a classic), say so. Asking 'can I check that?' and grabbing the paperwork is fine. Faking it is not.
Where Things Go Wrong

Five out of six rejections come from the same handful of preventable mistakes. The sixth is harder. Tap each pitfall below to see the symptom (what Amazon's email says), the root cause (what actually happened), and the fix.
If You Get Suspended

A small percentage of accounts get suspended during verification rather than rejected. Suspension is recoverable but requires writing a formal Plan of Action: a short document explaining what happened, why it happened, and what you are doing to prevent it. Plans of Action are written in three numbered sections (Root Cause, Immediate Action, Long-Term Action) and are submitted via the Performance > Account Health page.

Keep the Plan of Action factual and short. Two paragraphs per section is more effective than two pages. Amazon's response time is typically 48 hours for a first review. If the first plan is rejected, you can revise and resubmit. Do not appeal to multiple support cases in parallel; that just confuses the queue and slows your reinstatement.

blocks.label: Seller Central Tour
blocks.description: Section by section through the dashboard you will use every day. What lives where, and when you reach for it.

blocks.content: Your Operations Cockpit

Seller Central is Amazon's web app for sellers. It is where you list products, manage inventory, see sales, run advertising, file support cases, and watch your account health. Once verified, you will spend more time in Seller Central than on any other part of Amazon's site.

The dashboard can feel overwhelming on day one. There are eight top-level menus, each with five to fifteen sub-pages, and Amazon updates the layout every few months. The good news: you will only routinely use four of the menus, and the others you visit once a quarter. Knowing which is which saves an enormous amount of time.
The Eight Menus You Will Actually Use

Tap each menu in the sidebar below to see what lives inside it, what it does, when you reach for it during the normal week, and what to watch out for. The first four (Catalog, Inventory, Orders, Performance) are your daily drivers. The other four are reference and occasional use.
Where to Spend Time Each Week

A healthy weekly rhythm looks like this. Daily, 5 minutes: glance at the home dashboard for any red banner, scroll the Orders feed for unusual activity. Twice a week, 15 minutes each: review Inventory for stockouts and Performance > Account Health for any new warnings. Weekly, 30 minutes: run a Sales report, compare to the previous week, note anything anomalous. Monthly, 90 minutes: full close, pull the Payments report, reconcile against your bank, file the figures for your accountant.

That cadence keeps you ahead of every metric Amazon cares about without becoming a full-time Seller Central operator. Every minute spent outside that rhythm should be product research, sourcing calls, or new listing creation. Time inside Seller Central is overhead; time outside is what compounds.

blocks.label: Day-One Account Hygiene
blocks.description: The eight setup tasks that protect your account, your money, and your future sanity.

blocks.content: The Account Health Mindset

Once verified, you are responsible for keeping the account in good standing. Amazon does not warn you progressively as things degrade; it goes from green to amber to suspended quickly when a metric crosses a threshold. The fix is not vigilance; it is hygiene. A handful of small setup tasks done in the first hour after verification eliminate 80% of the situations that cause suspensions later.

Treat hygiene like the rest of the Elite FBA framework: front-load the discipline, then let the system run on its own. Once these eight tasks are done correctly, you will not touch most of them again for the life of the account.
Your First-Hour Setup

Three of the eight tasks below are critical and must be done on day one. Four are high priority and should be done within the first week. The last (Brand Registry) is parked for later, after your first bundle has validated and you have a trademark in progress. Tap any task to see exactly what to do, where it lives in Seller Central, and why it matters.
Building a Weekly Rhythm

After day-one setup, account hygiene takes about 15 minutes a week. Every Monday morning, check three things: Account Health (still green?), Inventory Performance (any new stranded SKUs?), and Notifications (any policy emails from the previous week?). If everything is clear, close the tab and get back to product research. If something is amber, fix it the same day.

🎯 The Compounding Effect: a clean account on day 365 is a direct result of clean hygiene on day 1. There is no way to retroactively fix a suspended account except to write a Plan of Action. Prevention is roughly fifty times cheaper than cure.
With the account open, verified, and properly set up, you are ready for Module 3, where we move from operations to product research and start finding the bundles that will actually fund the business.
Module 3: Finding Bundles That Sell

blocks.label: The Research Mindset
blocks.description: How to think about product research: what makes a viable bundle candidate before you even open Amazon.

blocks.content: Why Most Product Research Fails

Most people who try to find products to sell on Amazon spend weeks looking and never source a single unit. They scroll through hundreds of items, get excited about half a dozen, do five minutes of half-hearted Amazon checking, and end up frozen by the choice. The problem is not the volume of products. The problem is they have no clear definition of what a good candidate even looks like, so every product feels equally promising and equally risky.

An operator has the opposite experience. They walk into a shop with a mental filter dialled in tight, scan an aisle in 60 seconds, and either flag one or two items for closer investigation or move on without taking a single photo. They miss things, but the things they catch are real. The filter is the entire game.

🎯 The Operator Reframe: research is not about finding the perfect product. It is about quickly rejecting the 98% of products that will not work, so you can spend real time validating the 2% that might.
The Two Bundle Routes

Every bundle we build sits in one of two categories, and recognising the difference upfront saves a lot of confused research. Route one is the multi-pack: three of the same item packaged together, like a 3-pack of the same pet food. The customer benefit is convenience and a small discount versus buying singles. Route two is the complementary pair: two genuinely different products that solve the same problem together, like pet food and dental sticks. The customer benefit is curation: someone else has picked the right pair so they do not have to.

Multi-packs are easier to build (one SKU to source) but face more competition because the maths is obvious to other sellers. Complementary pairs are harder to design (you have to know which items genuinely go together) but the resulting ASIN is more defensible because the curation itself is intellectual property. We use both, but we lean towards multi-packs for the first three to five listings to get the rhythm of operations down.
The Pre-Validation Gate

Before we sink 20 minutes into the full Amazon Validation Method (Lesson 3), we run every candidate through a three-gate pre-check. Each gate is a single question that can be answered in under five minutes. Fail any one of them and the candidate is dead; there is no point investigating further. The gates exist because most candidates die at one of these three points anyway, so doing the cheap test first saves the expensive test.

Gate one asks whether the product can plausibly be sold as a multipack at all. Gate two asks whether someone else has already built that multipack and locked the listing position. Gate three asks whether the brand itself is off-limits because the manufacturer dominates its own Amazon presence. Pass all three and you have earned the right to run the full validation method.
The Big Brand Trap

Gate three is the one most new sellers miss, so it deserves a closer look. The brands you instinctively recognise from television adverts (L'Oreal, Garnier, Maybelline, Nivea-by-Beiersdorf, Procter & Gamble lines like Pantene and Head & Shoulders, Unilever lines like Dove and Vaseline, Reckitt lines like Dettol and Veet, Nestle confectionery) are almost all already on Amazon in a serious way. They have direct relationships with Amazon Retail, which means Amazon itself buys at the lowest possible wholesale tier and sells the product on its own Buy Box. They run Brand Stores that customers click into. They run Sponsored Brands ads at the top of every relevant search. They have A+ content on every listing.

For a new third-party seller trying to launch a bundle, this is a hostile environment. Even if you can source the product cheaply enough to build a bundle, you cannot win the visibility fight. Amazon Retail will undercut your single-unit price. The Brand Store funnels search traffic away from your listing. Sponsored Brands ads at the top of the SERP eat the first 10% of clicks before any organic result is seen. Your bundle launches into a search page where the brand owns the top three rows of pixels.

The brands you want to target sit in the opposite position. They are usually mid-sized or specialist: well-established at retail in Boots, B&M, Home Bargains, Holland & Barrett, independent pet shops, and local mini markets, but with no aggressive direct-to-Amazon programme. Examples of the profile we look for: Dr. Beckmann, Childs Farm, KMS, NYX (depending on category), Sukin, Vosene, Astonish, Pedigree treats, regional health food brands, niche pet specialists, smaller cosmetics labels. These brands distribute through a third-party UK distributor (which is where you buy wholesale from in Module 3 Lesson 6) and leave the Amazon channel mostly to third-party sellers. That is the gap.

🎯 The Recognition Test: if you can name the brand without thinking about it, and you have seen its adverts on TV, walk away. If you only recognise the brand because you walked past it in B&M last week, that is the right altitude for a new operator.
The Mental Model: A Funnel, Not a Search

Think of research as a funnel. The top of the funnel is everything on a shop shelf and every product on Amazon's catalogue. The middle is the small subset that clears the pre-validation gate. The narrow end is the handful that pass the Amazon validation method (Lesson 3) and the Bundle Scorecard (Lesson 5). Your job is to move products through the funnel quickly, not to fall in love with any single item near the top.

The numbers we expect at each stage, roughly: 200 products glanced at in a session, 20 to 30 photographed for closer look, 8 to 12 validated on Amazon in detail, 2 to 4 scored, 1 actually sourced. If you find yourself with a 50% pass-through rate at any stage, your filter is too loose. Tighten it.

blocks.label: Sourcing Hunting Grounds
blocks.description: The physical shops and online directories where bundle opportunities actually live.

blocks.content: Why Physical Shops Beat Spreadsheets

Almost every new seller starts product research by opening a spreadsheet, downloading an Amazon best-sellers report, and trying to reverse-engineer a winning product from data alone. It rarely works. The data tells you what is already selling well on Amazon, which means by definition the competition is already established. The interesting opportunities are upstream: products that sell well at retail but have weak or non-existent bundle representation on Amazon.

You find those opportunities by walking shops. You will spot products you did not know existed, brands you had never heard of, and pricing arbitrage that does not show up in any data tool. Every successful Elite FBA bundle started with someone noticing something in a physical aisle.
🎯 The Operator Routine: walk three or four shops a week, even when you do not need to source. The discovery muscle gets weaker if you do not use it. Treat it like a runner treats easy mileage.
Where to Hunt and What to Look For

Different hunting grounds give you different signals. Boots and Superdrug are brand-discovery shops where you walk the shelves at full retail to learn which third-party brands sit in our target categories, then chase the wholesale relationship. B&M and Home Bargains are discount retailers that consistently carry mid-sized UK brands, where we spot the likes of Dr. Beckmann, Astonish, and Childs Farm rather than buying stock to flip. Poundland and Savers surface mini-sized branded basics that bundle naturally into 3-packs. Local mini markets and independent corner shops reveal which brands the accessible cash-and-carry wholesalers are actually supplying in small case quantities. Specialist shops surface niche brands with passionate customers.

Tap any hunting ground below to see what to look for, what your scan routine should be, and what to avoid. We are listing both physical and online sources; both matter. Online discovery (especially reverse-searching Amazon for products that need a bundle) feeds physical research and vice versa.
Reading the Back of the Packaging

While you are walking the shops, get into the habit of turning every promising product over and reading the small print on the back. UK packaging law requires every consumer product to display the name and address of the company importing or distributing it. That single line of small text is the most reliable starting point for a wholesale conversation, because it tells you exactly which UK business is already supplying that brand in case quantities.

The wording is usually one of three forms. 'Distributed in the UK by [Company Name]', 'Imported by [Company Name]', or 'For UK enquiries contact [Company Name]'. The company name will almost always have a website that surfaces in the first Google result, and from there you have a real business with a real email address that you can approach in Lesson 6 for wholesale pricing on larger ongoing quantities.

Build a simple capture habit. Photograph the back of every product you photograph the front of. Note the distributor company name in your research log alongside the brand, the shop you saw it in, and the date. Within a few weeks of walking shops you will have a short list of UK distributors that come up again and again across different brands, and those repeat names are the wholesalers worth prioritising. The same distributor often supplies a whole portfolio of brands, which means one good supplier relationship can unlock multiple future bundles.

💡 Tactical tip: photograph the back panel in good light and zoom in on the small print. The text is often three or four points smaller than the rest of the label. A quick crop on your phone makes it easy to read later when you sit down for your distributor research session.
Building Your Weekly Loop

A workable weekly research rhythm looks like this. Two physical shop visits, 30 minutes each. One Amazon reverse-discovery session, 45 minutes. One distributor research session, 30 minutes. That is roughly two and a half hours a week. From that you should be surfacing 4 to 8 candidate products that clear the pre-validation gate.

Keep a research log. A simple note on your phone is fine. For each candidate, jot: shop name, brand, product, your photographed price, your gut take on which trait might fail, and the date. Revisit the log weekly. Patterns will emerge: certain shops produce more candidates, certain categories dominate your wins, certain price bands feel right.
💡 Take photos, not notes, in store. The product photo encodes the price tag, the packaging, the brand, and a visual cue for size. Notes lose half of that and slow you down.

blocks.label: The Amazon Validation Method
blocks.description: Six-step Amazon search workflow that decides whether a candidate is worth bundling or not.

blocks.content: From Candidate to Confirmed Opportunity

A product that clears the pre-validation gate from Lesson 1 is a candidate, not an opportunity. To confirm it is actually worth your sourcing capital, you run it through the Amazon Validation Method: a six-step search-and-analyse routine that takes about 20 minutes per product and tells you definitively whether the market is open, crowded, or dead.

Each step gives you a single piece of evidence: does the single-unit listing exist, how many sellers compete on it, what is the current price, how fast is it selling, does a bundle already exist, and what would your bundle have to charge to clear the floor rule. Six pieces of evidence, six chances to spot a deal-breaker.
Reading Single-Unit Demand

The single-unit Amazon listing is your demand proxy. If shoppers are buying singles at meaningful volume, they will absolutely buy a 3-pack at a small discount. If shoppers are not buying singles, your bundle will not magically conjure demand. So the first three validation steps all read different angles on single-unit demand: existence, competition, and price stability.

The trick is not to over-interpret any single signal. A single-unit listing with 50 sellers might look hopelessly crowded, but if your bundle is unique you are not joining their fight at all; you are building a parallel listing. Conversely, a single-unit listing with one seller and a slowly declining price might look uncrowded, but if it is selling at a loss your bundle will too. Read all six signals together.
The Six-Step Workflow

Tap each numbered step below to see exactly what to do, what you should see on Amazon, the green-light conditions that mean continue, and the red-light conditions that mean stop. A full pass takes about 20 minutes for an experienced operator; double that on your first few attempts. Speed comes from repetition.

🎯 The 10:1 Rule: expect to reject 10 candidates for every one that clears all six validation steps. If your pass-through rate is higher, you are being too generous with red flags. If it is lower, your initial filter from Lesson 1 was too loose.
What Validation Does Not Tell You

The validation method tells you whether demand exists and whether the listing economics work. It does not tell you whether you can actually source the product at scale, what the customer reviews say about reliability, or whether there is a hidden quality issue with the brand. Those questions come up later in the Scorecard (Lesson 5) and the wholesale conversation (Lesson 6). Validation is a necessary but not sufficient gate.

blocks.label: Helium 10 X-Ray
blocks.description: The free Chrome extension that overlays sales estimates, BSR, and revenue on every Amazon search.

blocks.content: How to Install and Use Helium 10 X-Ray
The Only Third-Party Tool We Use

We try to keep the toolstack lean. There are dozens of paid Amazon research platforms (Jungle Scout, Viral Launch, SellerApp, ZonGuru, Keepa Premium) and most of them duplicate what the others do. Of all of them, the single tool that adds real value at the research stage and is genuinely free is Helium 10's Chrome extension, specifically the X-Ray feature.

X-Ray overlays a small data panel on top of any Amazon search results page. The panel shows estimated monthly sales, estimated monthly revenue, current Best Seller Rank, review count, and a listing quality score for every visible result. You see the entire competitive landscape of a search in one view, without having to click into each listing.

💡 We use the free tier only. The paid Helium 10 plans add keyword research and listing optimisation tools that are useful in Module 4 and Module 7, but for product research the free X-Ray feature is enough.
Setup and Tour

Four-step setup gets you up and running in about 10 minutes. Install the Chrome extension, create a free Helium 10 account, optionally connect it to Seller Central for later use, and pin the extension to your browser toolbar. From there, every Amazon search page becomes a research dashboard.

The walkthrough below covers the four setup steps and the six X-Ray metrics you will use during validation. Each metric tells you something specific about the niche; learning to read them as a group is the difference between research that feels rigorous and research that is rigorous.
How We Use X-Ray in Practice

The most useful workflow: take a candidate brand from Lesson 2, run a broad Amazon search for the brand or the category (for example, 'shampoo 250ml' or 'protein bar multipack'), and let X-Ray paint the landscape. Look at the top 10 results. Are they doing 200+ units/month each? Are there any obvious bundle listings, or only singles? Does Helium 10 estimate the listing quality scores below 7, suggesting room to compete on optimisation alone?

X-Ray is best treated as a sanity check, not a primary discovery tool. The candidates that survive your shop-floor filter and the Amazon validation method should also look healthy in X-Ray. If they do not, you missed something earlier. If they do, the green light is now triple-confirmed.

⚠️ Helium 10's sales estimates are estimates. They are accurate within roughly 20% on most listings but can be off by 50% on small-niche or low-velocity items. Never make a sourcing decision on a single X-Ray number; always cross-reference with BSR and review count.

blocks.label: The Bundle Opportunity Test
blocks.description: Five-criterion scorecard that decides whether a validated product becomes a sourced bundle.

blocks.content: From Validated Product to Sourced Bundle

By this point in the funnel, a product has cleared the pre-validation gate (Lesson 1), passed the six-step Amazon validation method (Lesson 3), and looks healthy in Helium 10 X-Ray (Lesson 4). That is still not enough to spend money on. The final gate is the Bundle Scorecard: five criteria that confirm the bundle has a clear economic case, a sourcing route, and a market position that does not already exist.

Each criterion is binary: it passes or it fails. There is no partial credit. A bundle that fails even one criterion is not necessarily dead, but it requires explicit rework on the failing axis before sourcing. A bundle that fails three or more is dead; do not try to salvage it. The temptation to push through a marginal candidate because you have already done so much work on it is the single most expensive bias in this entire business.

🎯 The Sunk Cost Trap: every hour you have already spent on a candidate is gone whether you source it or not. The only question that matters is whether the next pound spent has a positive expected return. If the scorecard says no, you save the next pound.
The Five Criteria

Tap each criterion below to confirm or fail it for your candidate. The verdict at the bottom updates live as you go. Aim for five out of five on your first sourced bundle. Conditional Gos (four out of five) are workable once you have two or three bundles under your belt; do not start on one.
Designing the Bundle Itself

Once a bundle passes the scorecard, the last design decision is composition: how many units, what specific variant, and how it physically packages. Three rules of thumb. First, 3-packs sell better than 2-packs because the visual gap with the single unit is bigger; the customer feels like they are getting an obvious deal. Second, the bundle should include the highest-velocity variant the brand offers, not the obscure one you happen to have stock of. Third, design the packaging to be flat and tight; size tier is fee tier.

For complementary pairs, the second item should solve the same problem as the first, not a different one. A shampoo and a matching conditioner pair well because they are both addressing hair care. A shampoo and a body wash pair worse because the customer is now solving two problems at once and may not need both this month.

💡 Pricing the bundle: take the single-unit Amazon price, multiply by the unit count, subtract 10 to 15%. That is your initial retail price. You can fine-tune from there once the listing is live and you see how customers respond.

blocks.label: Approaching Wholesale Suppliers
blocks.description: How to find the right distributor and run the email conversation from cold contact to first order.

blocks.content: Why Wholesale Beats Retail Past Validation

Retail sourcing is how you validate. Wholesale is how you scale. Once a bundle has proven demand at retail-sourced prices, the next move is to cut the component cost by 30 to 50% by buying directly from the brand's UK distributor. That margin lift compounds across every future sale and is what turns a single tested bundle into a long-running cash-flow engine.

Wholesale conversations intimidate new sellers because there is no public marketplace; you have to find the right contact and start the dialogue from scratch. The good news is that the format of the conversation is predictable. A handful of email templates and a clear understanding of what the supplier is looking for in your enquiry will get you through 90% of supplier interactions.

Before we dig into the tactics, one important point on who the wholesale conversation is open to. Approaching most UK wholesale suppliers is a business-to-business transaction. Distributors invoice a registered company, send a wholesale rate card based on case quantities, and deliver to a commercial address. Most will not open a trade account for an individual without a registered business. Below are the two routes through this lesson depending on where you are right now.
Route A: If You Already Trade as a Limited Company

If you already have a UK limited company set up with a business bank account, you can work through the rest of this lesson exactly as written. Suppliers will ask for your company registration number, a VAT number where applicable, and the trading details of where you intend to resell. You can answer all three immediately, which means you can move straight to outreach. Skip ahead to 'Finding the Right Contact' below and start your conversations this week.

If you do not yet have a limited company, you are not blocked from sourcing wholesale. Module 6 covers the entire company formation, trademark, and Brand Registry process step by step, and that is where most students set up the legal entity that the wholesale conversation requires. We do not introduce that work earlier on purpose: the validation in Modules 1 to 3 is deliberately set up to be doable as an individual, so you can prove the concept works for you before paying to incorporate.

🏢 The shortest path to direct wholesale: Module 6 takes about a fortnight of waiting time plus one focused afternoon of paperwork. If your bundle has cleared the Scorecard and you want to go direct, you can jump to Module 6 now, come back here once your company is registered, and pick the wholesale lesson back up without losing momentum.
Route B: If You Are Still Sourcing as an Individual

If you do not yet have a registered business and are not ready to set one up, there is a route that lets you keep validating and scaling without the wholesale conversation stalling. I am happy to approach the supplier on your behalf through my own limited company, place the order under my trading name, and then invoice the stock onward to you at the wholesale price plus a small handling cost. From there, you receive the inventory, send it into FBA under your own Amazon seller account, and run the listing as normal.

The process is simple. You identify the supplier and the SKUs using the methods covered in this lesson. You send me the details: brand, product, quantity, your target case size, along with a copy of any quote you already have. I contact the supplier, agree pricing and MOQ, place the order, and issue you a clean B2B invoice for the goods. You pay the invoice, and the supplier ships either to you directly or to my address for a quick handover onto yours.

This route exists specifically so that the wholesale economics covered in Module 3 are not gated behind incorporation. It is intended as a bridge until you finish Module 6 and set up your own limited company, at which point you start dealing with suppliers directly and the handover happens cleanly. Pricing is transparent: you see the supplier's invoice to my business, you pay that figure plus a flat handling rate, and the bulk of the margin you would have captured by being incorporated yourself stays with you.

💬 To take the individual-seller route, message me with the supplier name, the SKUs you want to order, and the quantity. I can usually have a B2B quote back to you within 48 hours and stock landed within two to three weeks of confirmation.
Finding the Right Contact

There are three reliable routes to the right distributor. Route one: the back of the product itself. UK packaging law requires the importer or distributor's name and address on every consumer product. Read the small print on the back of the bottle or box; you will often find a 'Imported by' or 'Distributed in the UK by' line with a company name. Search that company online for their website and email.

Route two: the brand's own website. Most brands have a 'Wholesale' or 'Trade' link in their footer. If they do not, look for a 'Contact' page and email asking who their UK distributor is. Brand reps will usually answer this honestly because it helps them place product. Route three: a Google search for 'BRAND NAME wholesale UK' or 'BRAND NAME distributor UK'. The first three results are almost always the right path; their websites will list available SKUs, minimum order quantities, and (for the well-run ones) a contact email for new account enquiries.

💡 If three different searches surface the same wholesale aggregator (esources, wholesaledomain, etc.), the aggregator is one level above the real distributor. Their pricing is barely below retail. Go one level upstream: ask the aggregator who they buy from, then contact that party directly.
Email Templates That Actually Get Replies

Tap each tab below to see the three templates that walk the full supplier conversation from cold contact through to placing the first order: First Contact, Follow-up, and Placing an Order. Toggle the annotations to see why each line is there. Swap the placeholders in braces for your own details before sending.
What Suppliers Look For

A wholesale distributor talking to a new Amazon seller is screening for three things, mostly without saying so. One: are you a real business or a hobbyist? They want to see a company number, a trading email on a real domain (or a clearly business-flavoured Gmail), and a tone that sounds like someone who has done this before. Two: are you going to break their pricing structure? They worry that you will undercut their other resellers on Amazon and damage the brand. Three: can you actually pay? An MOQ exists partly to filter out tyre-kickers.

Your job in the cold email is to pre-empt all three. Include company registration details. Mention that you maintain pricing discipline (you do not have to call it that; just framing your enquiry around bundle building rather than racing the Buy Box signals it). And offer to cover small costs like samples or shipping. None of these are expensive moves; together they signal that you are serious.
Cadence and Patience

Wholesale conversations move slowly. A typical timeline: cold email Monday, no reply by Friday, follow-up the following Wednesday, first response the week after, sample request and reply over the next ten days, terms agreement and first order in week four to six. Sometimes faster. Often slower. This is fine because by the time you are emailing suppliers, your test bundle is already validating on Amazon, so cash flow is not waiting on the wholesale conversation to close.

Do not pursue more than three to four supplier conversations at once. Each one needs real attention and your follow-up cadence falls apart at higher volume. Better to land one good wholesale relationship per month than to start ten and follow up on none.

🎯 The Long Game: a single strong wholesale relationship can supply you for years. Treat the conversation as the beginning of a multi-year partnership, not a single transaction. Your tone in the first email sets the tone for everything that follows.
With your first bundle validated, scored, and supplied, you are ready for Module 4: turning the bundle into a published Amazon listing that customers actually find and buy.
Module 4: Listing Creation

blocks.label: Anatomy of a Listing
blocks.description: What the Amazon listing form is asking for and the three jobs each part has to do.

blocks.content: What a Listing Actually Is

An Amazon listing is the single page a customer sees when they click into your product. It is also the database entry that Amazon's search algorithm reads to decide when and where to show that page. Most new sellers spend their first listing thinking of it as a marketing brochure, when in reality it is two things at once: a sales page for the human visitor and a structured record for the machine. The fields you fill in this module have to satisfy both audiences.

Across this module we work through the listing creation flow end to end. Lesson 2 covers the generic-brand path and the GTIN exemption that lets you publish without a barcode. Lesson 3 covers writing the listing copy with AI help. Lesson 4 covers converting the description to HTML so it actually renders well on Amazon. Lesson 5 covers the seven image slots. Lesson 6 walks through the remaining form fields including dimensions, compliance, and pricing. By the end you have a live listing ready to receive inbound stock in Module 5.
The Three Jobs Every Listing Has to Do

Every part of a listing exists to do one of three jobs. Job one: get found. The title, search terms, and BSR all feed Amazon's search index, deciding whether a customer typing 'stainless steel cutlery set' ever sees you. Job two: get clicked. The main image and the price are what convert a search impression into a click into your page. Job three: get bought. The bullets, description, A+ content, and reviews are what convince the customer who clicked to add to basket.

A weak listing usually fails one of those three jobs cleanly. Tap through the anatomy below to see which part of the listing does which job. You will refer back to this map several times in the next five lessons.
Iterative, Not One-Shot

Your first listing will not be perfect. It is not supposed to be. Spending three weeks polishing a listing before publishing wastes time you could be using to gather real customer behaviour data. The right mindset is to publish a clean v1 that meets every compliance requirement, then iterate based on actual conversion data over the first month. Module 7 covers iteration in depth; for now, the goal is a publishable v1.
🎯 The Publishing Standard: every field is filled, every image meets spec, every required declaration is correct. That is the bar for v1. Beauty and polish come later from data, not from your gut.

blocks.label: Generic Brand & GTIN Exemption
blocks.description: Listing under Generic without a barcode, and walking through the GTIN exemption application.

blocks.content: Why We List Under Generic

By default, Amazon expects every product to carry a GTIN: a Global Trade Item Number, which on most consumer goods is the UPC or EAN barcode printed on the packaging. For a brand-new bundle that you have created yourself, no GTIN exists. You could buy one from a barcode reseller for around £30, but for a v1 test listing that is money you do not need to spend. Amazon offers a GTIN exemption specifically for sellers in your position: new bundles, generic-branded products, and small-batch sellers who do not yet have a registered trademark.

Listing under the 'Generic' brand is the path we take in Module 4 because it removes three obstacles at once. You do not need a registered trademark. You do not need a barcode. You do not need Brand Registry. All three of those come later: Module 6 covers the trademark and brand setup, after you have proven the bundle works. For now, Generic is the fastest legal route to a published listing.

🏷️ Generic is a real brand on Amazon. It is not a workaround or a loophole. Thousands of legitimate sellers list under Generic permanently. The only thing you lose is Brand Registry, which you do not need to launch and validate.
What You Need Before You Apply

The exemption application is entirely online and entirely photo-based. There is no PDF letter, no brand authorisation document, no signature scan; Amazon only asks for a set of clear product photos. What those photos have to show is the important part. Amazon needs to see the product itself from a couple of angles, your chosen brand name visibly attached to the packaging in a way that cannot be peeled off, and no existing barcode anywhere on the product or its packaging.

Permanence is the bit that trips most people up. Amazon's reviewer needs to be confident that the brand name belongs to the packaging and cannot simply be peeled off and swapped later. The easiest way to demonstrate this without spending money on custom-printed packaging is the method I use myself: take a plain polybag or kraft box, print a sticker with your chosen brand name, and place the sticker INSIDE the bag with the product so that the sticker is sealed in when the bag is closed. A sticker stuck on the outside of the bag will be rejected because the reviewer assumes anything peelable is temporary. Three or four photos cover the whole application: one of the bundle itself, one of the packaging showing the brand sticker visible through or inside the bag, and one of the back of the packaging confirming there is no existing barcode.

The whole asset prep takes about twenty minutes of focused work. Take the photos with your phone in natural light against a plain background. The walkthrough below covers the application itself step by step.
After the Exemption Is Approved

Approval typically arrives inside 24 to 72 hours by email. Once approved, you go to Catalog → Add Products → I'm adding a product not sold on Amazon, type 'Generic' as the brand name, and the form will let you proceed without a barcode field. From here, the rest of the listing creation flow looks exactly like any other Amazon listing, which is what the next four lessons cover.

⚠️ If your exemption is rejected, the rejection email tells you exactly which check failed. The single most common reason is a brand-name sticker stuck on the outside of the packaging instead of sealed inside. Move the sticker so it is sealed inside the bag with the product, take fresh photos, and re-submit. Second applications almost always succeed.

blocks.label: Writing the Listing Copy
blocks.description: Drafting your title, bullets, and description with AI as a starting point.

blocks.content: First, Why Keywords Matter

Before we touch the title, bullets, or description, we need to cover why the specific words you put in them matter so much. If you have never come across the term SEO before, the concept on Amazon is simple. Amazon is a search engine, not a shop window. When a customer types something into the Amazon search bar, Amazon has to decide which listings to show them and in what order. The single biggest factor in that decision is whether the exact words the customer typed appear in your listing. Get those words right and your product appears on the first page of results. Miss them and your product is invisible, no matter how good the bundle is.

SEO stands for Search Engine Optimisation. On Amazon, all it really means is writing your listing in the language your customer uses when they search. A customer looking for a dining cutlery set does not type 'tableware metallic accessories'; they type 'cutlery set' or 'stainless steel cutlery set' or 'knife and fork set'. Each of those exact phrases is what we call a keyword. Your listing needs to contain the keywords customers actually use, otherwise you will never appear when they search, however polished your photos or pricing happen to be.
A Worked Example

Imagine you are launching a 24-piece stainless steel dining cutlery set for 6 people. Three different customers might search for that exact same product in three different ways: 'stainless steel cutlery set 24 piece', '24 piece cutlery set for 6 people', and 'knife fork spoon set 6 person'. All three are perfectly valid customer phrasings of the same buying intent. Your listing has three places it can hold keywords for Amazon to read: the title (which carries the most weight in the search algorithm), the bullet points (medium weight), and the backend search terms field (invisible to the customer but indexed by Amazon). Across those three places, you need to cover as many real customer phrasings as you can, weaving them in naturally rather than stuffing them in.
Where Your Keywords Come From

You do not have to guess what customers actually search for. That is exactly what Helium 10, the free Chrome extension you set up in Module 3 Lesson 4, surfaces for you. Open Helium 10 on the top-ranking competitor for your product, run a keyword research lookup, and you see a list of the actual search phrases driving traffic to that listing, along with how many people search each phrase per month. Take the top five to ten phrases that genuinely describe your bundle. Those are the keywords you weave into your title, bullets, and search terms field in the rest of this lesson. Further down this lesson you will also find an AI keyword-research prompt that gives you a quick brainstorm of customer phrasings even before you open Helium 10; treat the AI list as a fast starting point and the Helium 10 numbers as the validation. The title prompt then has a 'top keywords' field where you paste the phrases you have chosen, and the AI weaves them into the copy for you.

🎯 The keyword principle in one line: every word a customer might realistically type to find a product like yours should appear somewhere across your title, bullets, and search terms field. Not stuffed in. Not repeated five times. Just present, naturally, at least once.
Title, Bullets, Description: Three Different Jobs

The three pieces of listing copy each do a different job. The title is for the search algorithm: it is the field that decides whether you appear at all when a customer types a query. The bullets are for the scanner: a customer who has clicked into your listing but has not committed to read everything. The description is for the considered buyer: someone who is genuinely interested and wants more context before adding to basket. Writing them as if they were all the same kind of content is the single most common mistake we see in new listings.

A good workflow uses an AI assistant (ChatGPT, Claude, or any capable model) to draft each piece against a structured prompt. AI is good at producing a competent first draft fast. It is not good at making the small judgement calls that turn a draft into a converting listing, so you always read, edit, and tighten what comes back. The three prompts below give you a reliable starting point for each piece.
How to Refine AI Output

Treat the AI output as a 70% draft. Three editing passes turn it into something you can publish. Pass one: strip filler words. AI loves 'enjoy', 'experience', 'discover', 'revolutionary', 'unparalleled', 'cutting-edge'. Find and remove every instance; the sentences almost always read better without them. Pass two: read each bullet and the title aloud. If it sounds robotic when spoken, rewrite. Pass three: check every claim against the actual product. AI will happily invent a vitamin content, a certification, or an ingredient that is not really in the bundle. Cross-reference everything with the packaging in front of you.

Save the polished title, bullets, and description in a single document before you leave this lesson. The next two lessons (HTML conversion and images) build on top of this text, and you will paste the finished versions into Seller Central in Lesson 6.

💡 The two-prompt rule: never publish copy generated by a single AI prompt. Always run the output through a second 'critique and improve' prompt, then edit by hand. The first draft is shape; the second is voice; the third is yours.

blocks.label: HTML Description Formatting
blocks.description: Why HTML descriptions outperform plain text on Amazon and how to convert yours in one click.

blocks.content: Why HTML Beats Plain Text on Amazon

Amazon's description field has a specific quirk: it collapses plain-text line breaks into a single block of prose when it renders on the live listing. If you write three short paragraphs in the form, the customer sees one wall of text. This is not a bug, it is how the field works, and most new sellers do not realise until their listing publishes looking nothing like the document they wrote.

The fix is HTML. Amazon respects a small set of HTML tags inside the description: paragraphs, line breaks, bold, and a couple of others. Wrapping your text in these tags preserves the structure, gives you visual emphasis where you want it, and turns a wall of prose into a scannable mini sales page. Listings with HTML descriptions consistently outperform plain-text equivalents on conversion.
💻 You do not need to know HTML to do this. We use a free tool that converts your plain prose into Amazon-compatible HTML in one click. The tool link is below the comparison.
Plain vs HTML, Side By Side

The demo below shows the same description three ways. 'Plain text on Amazon' shows what your customers actually see if you paste prose into the field without conversion. 'HTML rendered' shows the same content with the right tags applied. 'HTML source' shows the actual tagged text you would paste into Seller Central.
The Free Conversion Tool

We use the SellerApp Amazon Product Description Editor, a free web tool that converts plain prose into Amazon-compatible HTML. The workflow is dead simple: paste your polished plain-text description into the left panel, click 'Convert', copy the HTML output from the right panel, and paste that HTML directly into the Description field in Seller Central. The whole conversion takes 30 seconds.

blocks.content: The tool gives you a few formatting buttons (bold, italic, paragraph break, bullet list) that you can use to add emphasis before clicking convert. Use them sparingly: two or three bold phrases per description, never a full sentence in bold. The goal is to draw the eye to the benefit headlines, not to shout.
